articles.title: DRDO develops portable system to sniff out enemy radars, track drone threats
articles.summary: The Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) is moving to develop man-portable electronic intelligence modules, a compact system meant to pick
articles.body: The Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) is moving to develop man-portable electronic intelligence modules, a compact system meant to pick up and analyse the signals that enemy radars or any other antennas emit. The tender has been issued by the Defence Electronics Research Laboratory (DRDL) located in Hyderabad. Electronic intelligence, or ELINT, is the practice of capturing signals from radars and other electronic equipment and studying them to work out what kind of system is operating and its technical characteristics are. A radar or an drone operator could be emitting signals, which could inform about the frequency range of the device sending out signals. This could help jam the system more effectively, focussing on those particular frequencies and thereby rendering the effectiveness of the system.The process begins with the antenna and receiver, which pick up signals across several frequency bands, since different radars work on different frequencies. The system then measures the signal's characteristics, including frequency, pulse width, the interval between pulses, the number of pulses sent in a given time, signal strength, direction of arrival and the modulation within the signal.In an operational area, several radars may be active at once and their signals reach the receiver together. Separating them is known as deinterleaving, and it relies on frequency, timing between pulses and other inbuilt features, with digital processing and machine learning used in modern systems. The separated signal is then compared with a library of known radar signatures, which lets the system judge what type of radar is being used to, be it a search radar, a tracking radar or a fire control radar. Search radars scan a wide area for targets, tracking radars keep watch on a particular target and fire control radars support the use of weapons.Portability for such a system is important, especially in mountainous and remote terrain, where deploying large vehicles or fixed surveillance equipment could be difficult. A small system can give field formations information on electronic activity without depending on assets available with larger platforms. In an era, where drones are taking centre stage, the deployment of such systems could help pinpoint the location of a drone operator or could give early waring of an approaching inimical drone, thus providing own forces more time to activate counter drone drills.The system can also estimate where a signal is coming from. If sensors at different locations pick up the same signal, their readings can be combined to estimate a location, using techniques such as triangulation and time difference of arrival of radar waves. Different digital techniques, helps analyse a signal by frequency. Once the signal is identified, the system assesses the threat and a change in a radar's signal may indicate that its mode of operation has changed.The DRDL project has three separate parts which are defined as development, integration and qualification. Development will cover the equipment and its modules, integration brings the parts together into one working system and qualification tests it against technical and environmental standards, including temperature, humidity, vibration, shock and electromagnetic interference.

articles.title: Jersey deputy calls for more food funding due to high living cost
articles.summary: Deputy Louise Doublet does not think the cost of living was considered in the ending of a trial.
articles.body:
A Jersey politician said she thought cost-of-living pressures were not considered by the government when it chose to end a trial of free fruit in primary schools.

Since 2024 children in four primary schools have been able to get apples, bananas and other fruit as part of the pilot scheme.

Deputy Louise Doublet said: "To have that taken away at a time when the cost of living is still increasing I think has been quite hard for some families".

The education minister ended the trial because not enough children were eating the fruit and it was leading to a lot of wastage. The Government of Jersey has been approached for a comment.

The government announced in September fresh fruit would be included in a school food programme that provides hot school meals for government primary schools.

Minister for Education and Lifelong Learning Catherine Curtis previously said the free fruit scheme was leading to "a lot of wastage" and parents "actually asked" for fruit to be incorporated into the school food programme instead.

The topic was debated 29 September in the States Assembly.

Doublet said the minister had responded to her questions in the assembly "centred around the evidence and she informed the assembly that it hadn't resulted in much of an increase in children actually consuming fruit and vegetables and I do accept that".

But she added she did not think benefits in terms of cost of living were measured by the scheme.

"Personally I would like to see more investment in healthy food especially if it's locally grown food to help families with the cost of living," she said.

When asked about the contract with UK company Apetito Limited to provide hot school meals for government primary schools across Jersey she said it was the "best available option".

She added she understood people's concerns around the freshness of the food but her "understanding is that the meals are actually frozen rather than artificially preserved".

"I would like to see these funded meals extended further because it hits the cost of living for parents and... provides healthy meals for children," she said.

articles.title: Cumbria support group opens up conversation on menopause and pain
articles.summary: Menopause Matters is holding a county-wide online forum on Sunday for World Menopause Day.
articles.body:
A support group is holding a county-wide event for women coping with pain associated with menopause and perimenopause.

South Cumbria support group Menopause Matters is holding an online forum for World Menopause Day, inviting people to share their experiences and ask questions.

World Menopause Day is an annual event started by the International Menopause Society (IMS), with this year's theme Chronic Pain At Midlife.

Facilitator Leigh Williams said she hoped Sunday's free online event, being held between 19:00 and 20:00 BST, would "open up the conversation" around pain and menopause.

Menopause Matters also holds a monthly cafe-style drop-in in Barrow-in-Furness, offering women the opportunity to meet up in an informal environment.

Williams was inspired to become a facilitator because of her own experience with perimenopause and chronic pain.

"I know what it feels like when pain starts to shrink your world," she said. "Some of the women that come to the support groups are really desperate for an outlet, they haven't been able to talk about these topics or get the support that they wanted."

The online session will bring together a number of professionals and personal perspectives on menopause, and will be an open conversation format rather than a traditional webinar or expert panel.

Participants will include a GP, pelvic health physiotherapist, local authority health professional, support group facilitators and people with lived experience of persistent pain.

"What we've seen through the menopause cafe is that women's experiences don't fit neatly into boxes," Williams said. "We might start with menopause and very quickly find ourselves talking about pain, sleep, mental health, stress or neurodiversity.

"No one person on this call has all the answers. That is exactly why we're bringing different perspectives together."

According to the International Menopause Society, almost three in four women experience joint or muscle pain during perimenopause, while women are up to 70% more likely than men to experience chronic pain generally.

Some of the common symptoms of perimenopause and menopause are painful, similar to musculoskeletal pain or symptoms of ﬁbromyalgia. They can include muscle and joint aches, stiffness and swelling, reduced strength and pins and needles.

"Menopause is something that effects 50% of the population, so we absolutely should be expecting a level of health," Williams added.

"Some women can be experiencing these symptoms for a decade - that's a long time to be uncomfortable.

"Health and wellbeing isn't just the absence of ill-health, it's about being able to thrive and that's what I'm striving for."

Anyone wishing to take part in the free online conversation can do so by reserving a space on the event's booking website .

articles.title: Is it safe to upload photos of your child to AI?
articles.summary: Experts warn photos uploaded to AI may be stored, reused or expose children's data.
articles.body:
Experts are urging parents to think carefully before uploading photographs of their children to artificial intelligence (AI) tools, amid concerns over how images could be stored, reused or shared.

The warning comes as some parents have been using AI to remove watermarks from school photos to avoid paying for them.

While specialists say AI can bring benefits, they urge families to check how platforms handle uploaded images and whether photographs may be used to train AI models.

"It's not about avoiding AI altogether," said George Martin, security and data protection adviser at South West Grid for Learning. "It's about understanding what happens to those images once they've been uploaded."

What happens when you upload a photo to AI?

AI tools are increasingly used to edit photographs, generate images, translate documents and help with everyday tasks.

Supporters say the technology can save time and improve accessibility. However, questions remain about how platforms use the data people upload.

"Parents have limited visibility over what happens to the images once they're uploaded," Martin said.

"The second point is how that image could be used. An image of a child's school photograph could train a model."

Most platforms allow users to change settings to stop uploaded content being used for training, although these options vary between services.

Martin explained that it is possible to change the settings on the AI platform to instruct it not to use images to train models.

"Most AI platforms default to that if they can so it is important to have a look at those settings," he added.

Martin said AI could clearly bring benefits and value to schools, while helping staff deliver the curriculum and reducing workload, adding: "South West Grid for Learning has developed AI guidelines for schools and education establishments.

"We were keen to strike the balance between schools taking advantage of all of the benefits and value it can bring."

The debate reflects wider concerns about sharing children's photos online.

David Ellis, professor of behavioural science at the University of Bath, said people should not be frightened away from technology that can improve their lives.

However, he is sceptical about uploading children's photos to AI systems.

"I wouldn't do it. I say that in a blunt way," Ellis said.

"I make a distinction between a local system and a cloud system," he said.

"There are powerful AI systems that are disconnected from the internet and if you upload it to that it won't go anywhere.

"It's similar to considering whether you should put your children's photos on social media because ironically, they can be scanned by AI.

"People need to be clear about where the data goes. And AI companies need to make it clear.

Is it safe to upload photos of your child to AI?

Dr Simon Thorne, a senior computer science lecturer at Cardiff School of Technologies, urged caution when uploading identifiable images.

He said as a general rule, people should "never upload any personable identifiable photos".

"It's a terrible idea. It's a big risk," he said.

Thorne said users often have little visibility over how uploaded images are stored or reused.

Thorne added: "The dataset could get leaked online potentially and your material can be used to train future generations of the model.

"The image could be sold - you have no idea."

Why are parents using AI with school photos?

Some parents say they can understand why people are using AI to get school photos of their children without paying.

Rocío Thenmeyer, a mum from Bristol, said she had not used AI in this way, but the cost of buying the photos year on year made getting the genuine photos too expensive for some.

"It's either turning to AI or actually not spend the money on buying the pictures," she said.

"It's easy to do, there's plenty of AI tools that allow you to do that.

"I understand why we should be more careful with the images of our children on social media or the internet," she added.

"But if people decide, you know what, we already have all of our pictures on social media, we already use everything on the internet, we don't care about where pictures of our kids go, then I understand why they would."

Campaigners say photos uploaded online can be difficult to remove and may be reused in ways users did not expect.

Concerns have also grown as AI-generated imagery becomes more sophisticated.

A recent report published by the charity Internet Watch Foundation, which works to stop child sexual abuse online, shows that more AI-generated child sexual abuse images were found by them in the first six months of 2026 than all of 2025

"This is real. The impact and the trauma is real. What would a parent think if that was to happen to their child, when they upload the image of their child, if that was to appear in that inappropriate manner?" Martin said.

"Once the image is up there it's virtually impossible to have it removed. You can't. Once it's in there, that's it."

Martin said a lot of parents may not be aware that each photograph has its own metadata, particularly with school photographers.

"It contains information around where the photo was taken, it might contain information about the school," Martin said.

"That metadata can then be used by others who are also deploying AI to find out a whole amount of information about that child in the photograph, even where they go to school.

"There are those that could take advantage of having that information.

"Those images in the wrong hands can be misused, repurposed, to create synthetic child sex abuse material."

Avoiding images that show school uniforms, badges or locations

Understanding whether images are stored locally or on cloud servers

Martin added that it is important to build awareness of the dangers before considering uploading an image.

"What appears to be an opportunity to save a few pounds, the longer-term implications are considerable," Martin said.

articles.title: A Wyoming ranch grew from a 160-acre homestead into a 320-acre dude ranch; its owners sold it to the National Park Service with a lifetime estate agreement
articles.summary: Long before Grand Teton National Park became a major destination for visitors, White Grass Ranch in Wyoming’s Jackson Hole valley was part of a growing
articles.body: Long before Grand Teton National Park became a major destination for visitors, White Grass Ranch in Wyoming’s Jackson Hole valley was part of a growing industry built around the American West’s landscapes and ranching traditions. According to the National Park Service (NPS), Harold Hammond filed a 160-acre homestead claim in 1913. His partner, George Tucker Bispham, later developed an adjoining claim, and the two properties eventually formed a 320-acre ranch. By around 1919, White Grass was accommodating paying guests, initially in three log houses. Activities associated with the ranch included horseback riding, swimming and fishing, while its library and card room offered indoor recreation. In 1956, Frank Galey and his wife, Inge, sold the ranch to the NPS while reserving a lifetime estate that allowed the family to continue using the property for residential and guest-ranch purposes. After the ranch’s guest operation ended in 1985, its historic buildings were eventually rehabilitated for a different purpose: training people to preserve historic structures.White Grass Ranch history: how a homestead became a dude ranchDude ranching developed as cattle ranchers began welcoming paying guests who wanted to experience the Western lifestyle. The NPS’s account of dude ranching in Grand Teton National Park describes how ranches in Jackson Hole evolved to accommodate visitors while retaining elements of their agricultural operations. Rather than working as full-time ranch hands, guests could experience activities associated with ranch life in a setting shaped by mountains, open land and livestock.White Grass began as a homestead rather than a purpose-built tourist facility. In 1913, Hammond filed a claim for 160 acres in the Teton National Forest area. A log structure was built on the property that year, although the length of time Hammond lived in the Main Cabin is unclear. Bispham started improving adjoining land in 1915 and later established his own homestead there. Their separate claims received patents in 1920 and 1923, respectively, according to the NPS’s White Grass Ranch cultural landscape history. The partners developed the property gradually. By around 1919, they were accommodating guests in three log houses. White Grass subsequently became the third dude ranch established in what is now Grand Teton National Park. The ranch’s early development illustrates how homesteads in Jackson Hole could evolve from agricultural properties into businesses catering to visitors seeking recreation and an experience of Western ranch life.Bar BC Ranches, Inc. and the White Grass Ranch for BoysWhite Grass underwent a major change in ownership and use during the 1920s. Between 1923 and 1928, Hammond and Bispham transferred their claims to Bar BC Ranches, Inc., a partnership that included the two men as well as Struthers Burt, Horace Carncross, Irving Corse and Sinclair Armstrong. Burt and Carncross were founders of the Bar BC Ranch, linking White Grass’s ownership history to the wider dude-ranch industry in Jackson Hole. During this period, White Grass became known as the White Grass Ranch for Boys. Thirteen cabins were added to the three already in existence, and a concrete swimming pool was built in a hayfield. Young men, including visitors from eastern universities, spent parts of the summer learning traditional ranch skills and elements of self-reliance, according to the NPS.In 1928, Hammond and Bispham ended their partnership with Bar BC Ranches, Inc., and Hammond purchased the property, buildings and furnishings from Bispham. Hammond continued operating the 320-acre ranch over the following decade, combining guest accommodation with agricultural work. The NPS records that the ranch supported about 50 head of cattle under a grazing lease and that its operations included irrigation and haymaking. A separate bathhouse was also built, and bathrooms were later added to some guest cabins. These changes show that White Grass was not simply a holiday destination. Its operation continued to depend on the land, livestock and agricultural infrastructure that had shaped its early development.Frank Galey and the lifetime estate agreementAccording to the National Park Service, Hammond died in 1939, after which his stepson, Frank Galey, took over management of White Grass Ranch. The business was interrupted by the Second World War, when the ranch nearly shut down. Galey returned in 1946 and operated White Grass until his death in July 1985. The NPS describes it as the longest-lived active dude ranch in Jackson Hole. According to the National Park Service, Frank and Inge Galey sold White Grass Ranch to the agency in 1956 while reserving a lifetime estate agreement permitting continued family use of the property for residential and guest-ranch purposes. The arrangement meant that the federal government acquired the ranch while the family retained the right to use it during the lifetime-estate period. The ranch continued operating as a dude ranch until 1985, when Galey’s death brought the operation to an end and the lifetime estate expired.The National Park Service’s historical account states that, after Galey’s death, his second wife, Nora, hired an auctioneer to sell the ranch’s business assets. The park subsequently considered how to manage the property. During the late 1980s and early 1990s, several cabins were sold, water features and ranch fencing were removed, and the remaining buildings were boarded up as the initial management approach sought to return the site towards its natural condition.From guest ranch to historic preservation training centreWhite Grass Ranch later acquired a new role in conservation. In 2003, the National Park Service and the National Trust for Historic Preservation entered into an agreement to rehabilitate the historic ranch for use as a regional training centre. Preservation work began in 2005 and included repairs to foundations, roofs, windows and doors, the replacement of deteriorated logs, and improvements to ageing utility systems. The National Park Service announced the rehabilitation’s completion in December 2016, following 11 years of preservation work. According to the NPS announcement, White Grass became the home and primary training centre of the National Park Service’s Western Center for Historic Preservation. The site’s historic buildings now support training in techniques used to preserve traditional structures, including log buildings.The NPS and the National Trust jointly funded the rehabilitation, which cost approximately $3 million. The completed project adapted the surviving ranch buildings for a new use while retaining their historic character. Sleeping cabins provide accommodation for trainees, while the Main, Hammond and Bath House cabins serve as shared spaces for meals, teaching and practical work. According to the National Park Service, the White Grass Heritage Project was established in 2014 to collect oral histories, documents and photographs about life at the ranch. Former guests and wranglers have been invited to contribute their memories, preserving accounts of a business that operated for decades before closing in 1985. White Grass Ranch’s history reflects two different periods in Jackson Hole’s development. It began with homestead claims and agricultural work, grew into a dude ranch that welcomed visitors seeking a taste of Western life, and eventually became a site for teaching historic preservation. Its buildings remain part of the landscape, but their purpose has changed from accommodating holiday guests to helping protect historic structures elsewhere.You use AI every day. articles.title: Her sister died in a 47-car pile-up and the surviving children reached hospital unidentified; she turned the tragedy into a car-seat ID tag that becomes an emergency wristband
articles.summary: When a serious road accident happens, first responders must make urgent decisions while dealing with injured people, damaged vehicles and incomplete
articles.body: When a serious road accident happens, first responders must make urgent decisions while dealing with injured people, damaged vehicles and incomplete information. For children who cannot explain who they are, even basic details such as their names, allergies and emergency contacts can become crucial.That concern inspired the Roth ID Tag, a child-safety product designed to keep important information close at hand. Attached to a child’s car seat, the tag can be removed and converted into an identification wristband for use during an emergency. Its purpose is simple: help responders identify a child and access essential information when a parent or caregiver cannot speak for them. Behind the product is a deeply personal story involving a devastating road crash, two young survivors and a family determined to prevent another child from facing the same uncertainty.A winter crash exposed a painful gapOn December 23, 2022, a major multi-vehicle collision on the Ohio Turnpike left families dealing with the consequences of a severe winter-weather incident. Among those caught in the crash were Julie Roth and her two children, Ayla and Rory. According to the account behind the product, Julie died, while both children survived. In the confusion that followed, emergency crews faced the difficult task of helping injured people and moving survivors to medical care. The children were secured in their car seats, but with their mother unable to provide information, responders struggled to establish who they were.The problem did not end when they reached the hospital. Staff needed to identify the children and determine important details about their medical needs and family contacts. The account says hours passed before their identities could be confirmed and their father could be contacted. For the family, the experience highlighted a vulnerability that can arise during large-scale emergencies. A young child may be unable to communicate, a parent may be critically injured, and identification documents may be difficult to locate amid the wreckage. In such circumstances, even a small, accessible record of information could help reduce confusion. Julie’s sister turned that experience into the idea for the Roth ID Tag, aiming to make a child’s essential details easier for emergency personnel to access.How the Roth ID Tag worksThe Roth ID Tag is designed to remain attached to the fabric of a child’s car seat. Before using it, a parent or guardian fills in the designated area with relevant emergency information. Depending on the product’s instructions, this may include the child’s name, emergency contacts and important medical details. If a crash or another emergency separates a child from their caregiver, a first responder can remove the tag and use its tear-off section to create an identification wristband. The wristband is intended to keep key information with the child as they are moved between responders or taken for medical treatment.This matters because information written on a loose piece of paper can be misplaced, while details stored only in a caregiver’s phone may be inaccessible if that phone is missing or the adult cannot be reached. Keeping identification attached to the car seat gives responders a visible place to check. The product also includes a QR code. If the family has registered the child through the Roth ID Tag website, scanning the code can provide access to additional information. The usefulness of that feature depends on registration, connectivity and the information made available through the system, so it should complement rather than replace the details written on the tag.The idea is not to replace emergency medical procedures or official identification systems. Instead, it offers an additional tool that may help responders establish a child’s identity and contact family members during a chaotic situation.Why a small piece of information can matterEmergency teams routinely work under pressure, especially when several vehicles and multiple casualties are involved. Identifying a child quickly can help staff match the child with family members and communicate more effectively with caregivers. Accurate information about allergies or other medical concerns may also be relevant to care, although treatment decisions must still be based on professional assessment. Captain Wilhelm of the Bellevue Fire Department in Ohio has praised the concept, saying, “I can recall countless situations where the Roth ID Tag would have made the scenario more manageable.”The endorsement reflects a practical concern for emergency personnel: small measures that make information easier to find can be useful when time and attention are limited. However, a tag cannot guarantee faster identification or a particular medical outcome. Its value depends on whether it has been completed accurately, remains attached and can be read when needed.The product’s design has reportedly received attention from child passenger safety technicians associated with Safe Kids Worldwide, along with recognition for addressing a specific safety need. The supplied account also says that law-enforcement and fire departments, highway-safety organisations and transportation agencies in several states have endorsed it. Families considering the product should check the current details of any endorsement and follow the manufacturer’s instructions for safe attachment and use.Turning grief into a practical safeguardThe Roth ID Tag grew from a family’s experience of loss and the frightening uncertainty that followed for two surviving children. Rather than allowing that experience to remain only a painful memory, Julie Roth’s sister used it to develop a product aimed at helping other families prepare for emergencies. Its central principle is straightforward: when children cannot identify themselves, their information should be accessible to the people trying to help them. A clearly completed tag cannot prevent a crash, and it should never be treated as a substitute for a properly installed car seat, emergency planning or medical care. But it may provide first responders with a useful starting point when every detail counts.For parents and caregivers, the story is also a reminder to keep emergency contacts and essential medical information current, make sure trusted adults know where to find them, and ensure that children’s safety equipment is used according to its instructions. Sometimes, a small preparation made long before an emergency can help reduce confusion when a family needs answers most.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Navratri 2026 Ashtami date: October 18 or 19? Know when to perform puja and kanya pujan
articles.summary: If you’ve been scrolling through different Navratri calendars lately, you might have noticed something confusing: some places list Maha Ashtami on October
articles.body: If you’ve been scrolling through different Navratri calendars lately, you might have noticed something confusing: some places list Maha Ashtami on October 18, while others mark it down for October 19.It’s an easy thing to get tripped up by, but there’s a simple reason for it. Unlike standard calendars where a new day starts at midnight, Hindu festival dates are driven by lunar days, or tithis. A tithi can start at almost any time of day and often straddles two separate calendar dates.Here is why the confusion happens, which date you should actually follow, and how to plan your fasts and Kanya Pujan smoothly.Why the dates differAccording to the Drik Panchang, the Ashtami tithi actually begins on Sunday, October 18, at 8:27 AM (IST) and runs until Monday, October 19, at 10:51 AM.So, if you see October 18 listed somewhere, that calendar is just highlighting when the tithi officially kicks off. However, standard tradition follows the Udaya Tithi rule - meaning the date active at sunrise is considered the main day of observance.Because the Ashtami tithi is live when the sun rises on Monday morning, Monday, October 19, 2026 is the official day for observing Maha Ashtami.Key timings to keep in mind (Delhi / IST)Ashtami Tithi Begins: Sunday, October 18 at 8:27 AMAshtami Tithi Ends: Monday, October 19 at 10:51 AMMaha Ashtami Celebration & Fasting: Monday, October 19Navami Tithi Begins: Monday, October 19 right after Ashtami ends (10:51 AM) and continues through October 20Note: Lunar timings can shift slightly depending on where you live. If you’re organizing a puja or fast, it’s always a good idea to double-check your local city’s panchang.What nakes Maha Ashtami so special?Maha Ashtami is easily one of the most sacred and energetic days of the nine-night festival. It’s dedicated to Goddess Mahagauri, the eighth avatar of Maa Durga, who represents purity, grace, and inner peace. Devotees spend the day fasting, decorating their altars with flowers and sweets, and visiting local pandals or temples.For many families - especially across North India - Ashtami is synonymous with Kanya Pujan. Young girls (representing the divine feminine energy of Durga) are welcomed into homes, given a ritual foot-washing, and served a traditional feast of puris, suji halwa, and cooked black chickpeas (kala chana). They’re also given small gifts, bangles, or money as a mark of respect before the fast is broken.What about Maha Navami?Because Ashtami wraps up at 10:51 AM on October 19, Navami begins immediately afterward on the very same day and runs into October 20.Depending on your family’s traditions, you might perform Kanya Pujan on the morning of October 19 while Ashtami is still active, or wait until Navami. If you’re planning a havan or a specific family ritual, checking in with your family priest or local temple will help clear up any scheduling overlaps.Which date should you follow?If you need a straightforward answer for your calendar: plan your fasts, temple visits, and main rituals for Monday, October 19.As long as you align your plans with the sunrise timing of your local area, you can rest easy knowing you're celebrating on the right day according to tradition.Get the latest movie news, reviews, and celebrity updates. articles.title: Keerthy Suresh, Radhika Apte’s 'Akka' teaser out: 1980s gangster drama introduces Bhavani and Rudra; series to premiere on October 30
articles.summary: Actors Keerthy Suresh and Radhika Apte are set to share screen space in the upcoming series 'Akka', a gangster drama set in the 1980s.
articles.body: Actors Keerthy Suresh and Radhika Apte are set to share screen space in the upcoming series 'Akka', a gangster drama set in the 1980s.The makers shared the teaser for the series on Saturday to mark Keerthy's birthday. Along with the teaser, the makers also announced the premiere date.The teaser introduces Keerthy as Bhavand Radhika as Rudra, two women at the centre of the story. Their characters appear to hold positions of influence in Pernuru, where competing interests and differing views set the stage for a clash.'Akka' marks the directorial debut of Dharmaraj Shetty, who has also written the series. The story is set in Pernuru, a kingdom shaped by generations of women who built, governed and protected it, with tradition, power struggles and rivalries forming the backdrop.Take a lookSpeaking about the project on her birthday, Keerthy said the teaser launch made the occasion special and described Bhavani as one of the most distinctive characters she has played."The love I receive from the audience every year makes this day incredibly meaningful, and being able to celebrate it by unveiling the teaser of Akka, a project so close to my heart, feels truly special. Bhavani is one of the most unique and memorable characters I have had the opportunity to play," she said, as per a release.Radhika Apte added, "It's wonderful that the date announcement and the teaser drop of Akka have coincided with Keerthy's birthday. I am sure it is going to be lucky for us. Rudra is a fascinating character, driven by her own convictions and an instinct to challenge the world around her. What drew me to the series was the complexity of its characters and the tensions that emerge from their differing perspectives."Alongside Keerthy and Radhika, the series also stars Tanvi Azmi. Aditya Chopra, Yogendra Mogre and Akshaye Widhani serve as executive producers.'Akka' will premiere on October 30.
